name: Chinese
intro: Chinese mythology is not one book or one faith. It gathers Shang-era divination and ancestor offerings, Daoist ideas about cosmic order and immortality, Buddhist stories arriving from India, and countless local temple and family traditions. The earliest written traces are oracle-bone inscriptions from about 1250 BCE, but most familiar narratives were shaped much later. The Shan Hai Jing, a strange geography of mountains and seas, preserves gods and monsters; Han writers such as the compilers of the Huainanzi retold creation and flood stories; Ming novels turned older material into the adventures of Nezha and Sun Wukong. Heaven could be imagined as a bureaucracy, with a Jade Emperor, ministries and dragon kings, while local gods varied from village to village. The stories here are a selection, not a single canon.

timeline.label: Shang divination
timeline.note: Oracle-bone inscriptions record questions to royal ancestors and to Di, a high sky power. These are the earliest surviving Chinese written traces of religious practice.

timeline.label: Warring States and Han
timeline.note: Texts such as the Shan Hai Jing, the Chu Ci and the Huainanzi collect or retell creation, flood and hero stories, often from older oral traditions.

timeline.label: Buddhism and pilgrimage
timeline.note: Buddhist stories and deities enter China. The historical monk Xuanzang travels to India, and his journey later becomes the frame for the Monkey King's adventures.

timeline.label: Ming novels
timeline.note: Journey to the West and Investiture of the Gods turn older religious and folk material into long vernacular novels read across East Asia.

timeline.label: Local cults and festivals
timeline.note: Temple worship, ancestor rites and festivals honour a vast range of local gods, including dragon kings, city gods and immortals.

timeline.label: Modern study and retelling
timeline.note: Scholars compare textual and regional versions, while film, television, opera and games give the stories new audiences.

sources.title: Shan Hai Jing (Classic of Mountains and Seas)
sources.note: A composite text, compiled over centuries, describing strange lands, creatures, gods and rituals. It preserves some of the oldest surviving mythic material.

sources.title: Huainanzi
sources.note: A Han-dynasty philosophical compilation that preserves the best-known accounts of Nüwa repairing the sky and Hou Yi shooting the suns.

sources.title: Chu Ci, 'Tianwen' (Questions of Heaven)
sources.note: An ancient poem that poses a series of cosmological questions, including questions about the suns, the moon and the ordering of the world.

sources.title: Shujing, 'Tribute of Yu'
sources.note: A classical text describing Yu's work on the rivers and the ordering of the land; its historical layers are debated.

sources.title: Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian)
sources.note: Sima Qian's Han-dynasty history retells the flood and the Xia dynasty, combining earlier traditions with a political narrative.

sources.title: Journey to the West
sources.note: A sixteenth-century novel attributed to Wu Cheng'en, following the monk Tripitaka and his companions, including Sun Wukong.

sources.title: Fengshen Yanyi (Investiture of the Gods)
sources.note: A sixteenth-century novel that develops the story of Nezha, the dragon kings and the war between the Shang and Zhou.

sources.title: Sanwu Liji
sources.note: A third-century CE text, quoted in later encyclopedias, that provides the earliest surviving written form of the Pangu creation story.
